idiom_name: enum with parameterized cases + exhaustive match
implementation_notes: Scala 3's enum construct is the direct expression of the pattern: cases with parameters carry per-variant payloads, the compiler desugars the enum to a sealed abstract class extending scala.reflect.Enum, and a match over it is checked for exhaustiveness. Keep the cases in the enum's companion and construct them through smart apply/parse methods that validate, so even the case classes are not a back door for illegal payloads; exhaustive matches need no catch-all, and adding a case is reported at every match that does not handle it. Use the sealed-trait form only when a case needs structure the enum syntax cannot express.
code_sketch:
enum ConnectionState:
  case Disconnected
  case Connecting(initiated: Instant)
  case Connected(sessionId: String)

val summary = state match
  case ConnectionState.Disconnected     => "down"
  case ConnectionState.Connecting(at)   => s"connecting since $at"
  case ConnectionState.Connected(id)    => id   // exhaustive, no wildcard
pitfalls: A case _ arm compiles and defeats the exhaustiveness check; with -Xfatal-warnings (or -Werror) a non-exhaustive match becomes a build failure instead of a warning.

Enum cases are their own types (and case classes), so a caller can still use the constructor directly - give the payload fields private constructors or validate in the enum's companion when the invariant depends on the payload.

Java interop and reflection can bypass the language-level closure in edge cases, and the desugared companion exposes fromOrdinal which throws for an out-of-range ordinal - parse untrusted data through an explicit decoder.

variants.name: Scala 2 sealed trait with case classes
variants.idiom_name: sealed trait + final case classes / case objects
variants.implementation_notes: On Scala 2 the pattern is a sealed trait with one final case class or case object per legal shape: sealed means all direct subclasses must be in the same file, so the set is closed and match is checked for exhaustiveness (a non-exhaustive match is a warning unless -Xfatal-warnings makes it an error). Case classes supply the per-variant payload and structural equality; companion apply/parse methods that validate replace raw construction. Prefer the Scala 3 enum variant on new code - the sealed trait encoding is the same idea with more boilerplate, and the desugaring it produced is exactly what Scala 3 enums now generate.
variants.code_sketch:
sealed trait ConnectionState
final case object Disconnected extends ConnectionState
final case class Connecting(initiated: Instant) extends ConnectionState
final case class Connected(sessionId: String) extends ConnectionState

def describe(state: ConnectionState): String = state match {
  case Disconnected          => "down"
  case Connecting(initiated) => s"connecting since $initiated"
  case Connected(sessionId)  => sessionId
}
pitfalls: sealed is file-scoped: a variant in another file does not compile, so the model and all its cases must live in one file (and the file can grow large for rich domains).
Exhaustiveness is a warning in Scala 2 by default - without -Xfatal-warnings a newly added case compiles and falls through at run time.
Case class copy and apply are public: callers can create a variant with invalid payloads, so validation must live in the case class's require or in the companion factory, not in the consumer.
